notes.front: What is Design for Six Sigma (DFSS)?
notes.back: A methodology and set of practices for developing new products and processes that are robust, reliable and capable from the start.
notes.explanation: Its emphasis is on meeting customer requirements from the outset of a project, rather than fixing defects once the design is in use.
notes.example: Like planning a new kitchen around how the cooks actually move before it is built, instead of knocking walls down afterwards.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is DMADV?
notes.back: Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify: DMAIC’s sister roadmap for designing something new.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam says it is sometimes called DFSS itself. The source spells the third phase “Analyze”; this deck writes “Analyse”.
notes.example: Like planning a new customer help line from nothing, rather than fixing one that already runs badly.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is IDOV?
notes.back: Identify, Design, Optimise, Verify: the DFSS roadmap MoreSteam builds its design training around.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam names it as the roadmap DFSS uses where Lean Six Sigma typically relies on DMAIC. The source spells it “Optimize”.
notes.example: Like a four-stage plan for launching a new online booking service, ending with a check that it works as intended.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is quality function deployment (QFD)?
notes.back: A disciplined matrix method that turns the voice of the customer, their wants and needs, into operational requirements.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio rates it an effective way to find the critical-to-quality characteristics of products, services and transactional processes.
notes.example: Like translating “the coffee should be hot” into a serving-temperature range the café can measure.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Quality Function Deployment (QFD)”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Pugh matrix used for?
notes.back: Choosing between design concepts: each option is scored against criteria, and the one with the best combined score is selected.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio stresses having many options before detailed design begins, so the best can be picked from them.
notes.example: Like scoring four draft layouts for a new waiting room against cost, space and accessibility before choosing one.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “PUGH Matrix”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is robust design aiming for?
notes.back: A product or process little affected by the external conditions it meets in use: the less affected, the better.
notes.explanation: Something made under controlled conditions may, in customers’ hands, show failure modes never seen in the lab.
notes.example: Like a phone charger designed to work just as well in a freezing garage as in a hot kitchen.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 5.1.2 “What are the uses of DOE?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: The less a process or product is affected by external conditions, the better it is - this is called "Robustness" An item designed and made under controlled conditions will be later `field tested' in the hands of the customer and may prove susceptible to failure modes not seen in the lab or thought of by design.

notes.front: What does a design FMEA (DFMEA) quantify, in LeanOhio’s glossary?
notes.back: How severe and how frequent failures to meet the critical-to-quality characteristics, and so the customer-critical needs, would be.
notes.explanation: In LeanOhio’s chain, QFD links customer-critical needs to critical-to-quality characteristics, and that work leads on to the DFMEA.
notes.example: Like listing, before a new bicycle lock is made, each way its design could fail to keep a bike secure, and how bad and how likely each is.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Critical to Customer”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In DMADV, which phase comes straight after Analyse?
notes.back: Design.
notes.explanation: This is where DMADV parts company with DMAIC, which moves on to Improve at this point.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the last phase of DMADV?
notes.back: Verify.
notes.explanation: DMAIC ends with Control instead.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three DMADV phases share their names with DMAIC phases?
notes.back: Define, Measure and Analyse.
notes.explanation: The two roadmaps split only after Analyse: Design and Verify in DMADV, Improve and Control in DMAIC.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the first phase of IDOV?
notes.back: Identify.
notes.explanation: IDOV runs Identify, Design, Optimise and Verify, in that order.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which IDOV phase does MoreSteam’s design training single out, using advanced modelling before a process goes live?
notes.back: Optimise.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam describes the roadmap as iterative, and puts the weight on optimising the design before launch.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What trade does DFSS make, in MoreSteam’s account of its objective?
notes.back: More work now, so there is no rework later.
notes.explanation: Aligning a design fully with customer needs before it is finished cuts the chance of fixing defects after launch.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two things DFSS and Lean Six Sigma have in common, according to MoreSteam?
notes.back: Any two, among others: a strong customer focus, a data-driven approach, problem-solving roadmaps.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam also lists risk management with tools such as failure mode and effects analysis, and a culture of process improvement.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In LeanOhio’s glossary, what two things does QFD relate to each other?
notes.back: Critical-to-customer needs (its input) and the internal critical-to-quality characteristics that relate to them.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio stresses that a critical-to-customer need is not the same thing as a critical-to-quality characteristic.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Critical to Customer”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does designing an item to be robust call for, according to the handbook?
notes.back: A special experimental effort, such as stressing the item in the design lab to find the critical components.
notes.explanation: Stressing the item in the lab is how the components that matter to its performance are found.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 5.1.2 “What are the uses of DOE?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Designing an item so that it is robust calls for a special experimental effort. It is possible to stress the item in the design lab and so determine the critical components affecting its performance.

notes.front: A council will open a permit service that has never existed, so there is no current process to measure. Which roadmap fits?
notes.back: D: DMADV, for designing a new process, product or service.
notes.choices:
A) DMAIC
B) Plan-Do-Check-Act
C) 5 Whys
D) DMADV
notes.choicesExplained: A improves a process that already exists. B suits small, quick changes. C is a root-cause tool, not a design roadmap.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam’s rule of thumb: DMADV when building from scratch, DMAIC when improving what exists.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants to try a small, quick change to the wording of one reminder letter. Which approach does MoreSteam suggest for a change this size?
notes.back: B: Plan-Do-Check-Act, for changes too small to need a full DMAIC project.
notes.choices:
A) DMADV
B) Plan-Do-Check-Act
C) A full DMAIC project
D) IDOV
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are design roadmaps for building something new. C is more than a change this small needs.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam places Plan-Do-Check-Act as the simpler cycle for smaller, faster changes.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A claims process has run for years, has measurable data, and produces too many errors. Which roadmap fits?
notes.back: B: DMAIC, for improving an existing process.
notes.choices:
A) DMADV
B) DMAIC
C) Pugh matrix
D) IDOV
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are for designing something new. C is a tool for choosing between concepts, not a project roadmap.
notes.explanation: An existing process with measurable data is the typical case for a DMAIC project.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A design team has five candidate concepts for a new ticket machine and wants to score each against agreed criteria before choosing one. Which tool fits?
notes.back: A: a Pugh matrix, for concept selection by scoring options against criteria.
notes.choices:
A) Pugh matrix
B) Quality function deployment
C) Design FMEA
D) Control chart
notes.choicesExplained: B turns customer needs into requirements rather than choosing between concepts. C looks at how a design could fail. D monitors a running process.
notes.explanation: Concept selection by combined scores against criteria is exactly what the Pugh matrix is for.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “PUGH Matrix”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before designing a new bank app, a team must turn interview comments such as “I want it quick” into measurable requirements. Which method fits?
notes.back: B: quality function deployment, which turns the voice of the customer into operational requirements.
notes.choices:
A) Pugh matrix
B) Quality function deployment
C) Design FMEA
D) Control plan
notes.choicesExplained: A chooses between concepts already drawn up. C looks at how a design could fail. D keeps a running process under control.
notes.explanation: Interview comments are the voice of the customer, and QFD is the matrix method for translating them.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Quality Function Deployment (QFD)”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A design team following IDOV has identified what customers need and drafted a design. Which phase comes next?
notes.back: D: Optimise, the third phase of Identify, Design, Optimise, Verify.
notes.choices:
A) Verify
B) Identify
C) Control
D) Optimise
notes.choicesExplained: A is the last phase, after Optimise. B is already done. C is a DMAIC phase, not an IDOV one.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam’s training puts its weight on this phase, optimising the design through modelling before it goes live.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the job of DMAIC differ from that of DMADV?
notes.back: DMAIC improves a process that already exists; DMADV designs a new process, product or service.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam calls DMADV DMAIC’s sister method, so the phases start the same but the purpose differs.
notes.contrast: DMAIC: fix what exists. DMADV: build from scratch.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “What is the DMAIC Methodology?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is DMADV or IDOV “the” DFSS roadmap?
notes.back: No single one: MoreSteam says DMADV is sometimes called DFSS, and also says DFSS uses the IDOV roadmap.
notes.explanation: The DMADV remark is in MoreSteam’s DMAIC article and the IDOV one in its DFSS guide; both are roadmaps for designing something new.
notes.contrast: DMADV: Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify. IDOV: Identify, Design, Optimise, Verify.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When in a product’s life is DFSS applied, compared with Lean Six Sigma?
notes.back: DFSS: during design, before the product or process launches. Lean Six Sigma: typically on an existing process needing improvement.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam treats the timing of implementation as one of the main differences between the two.
notes.contrast: Lean Six Sigma starts from a working process; DFSS starts before one exists.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “A Beginner’s Guide: What is Design for Six Sigma?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
